**Patient Vignette: Dr. M., Age 62**

Dr. M. is a 62-year-old Latin American man, a psychiatrist who has practiced in a major city for over thirty years. He is single, lives alone, and presents for therapy after a colleague noticed a marked deterioration in his clinical notes and his increasing withdrawal from the hospital’s social functions. He is impeccably dressed for each session, his posture rigid, his voice low and measured. He speaks of his past as if recounting a case study of another man.

The story begins in the late 1980s. Dr. M. was a young physician in his home country, a nation then under a brutal military dictatorship. He was arrested not for political activism, but for treating a student activist who had been shot. The patient died in his clinic. Two days later, armed men in plain clothes came for him. He was taken to a detention center.

He describes the first hours with clinical precision: the hood placed over his head, the smell of stale sweat and diesel, the sound of a generator humming. The interrogation began. They wanted names, affiliations. He had none to give. What followed, he says, was a course in the systematic destruction of a person. He was beaten with rubber hoses on the soles of his feet, a technique that left no visible marks but made standing agony for years. He was subjected to mock executions, the cold metal of a pistol pressed to his temple while a man whispered the details of his own funeral. He was kept in a cell so small he could not lie flat, forced to stand for days. He was denied food and water, then given salted water to drink. The most terrifying element, he now realizes, was the unpredictability. He never knew when the door would open, what they would do, or if he would be taken to the "final room."

He was released after six weeks, a broken man in a functional body. He fled to the United States, rebuilt his life, earned his credentials, and began his psychiatric practice. For decades, he told no one. He constructed a fortress of routine and intellectualism. He saw his patients’ trauma, but never his own.

In the present, the fortress is crumbling. It began six months ago, when a new patient—a young man who had been tortured in his own country—was referred to him. Dr. M. listened to the man’s story, and for the first time, he did not feel professional distance. He felt a cold sweat break out on his back. His heart hammered. He ended the session early, claiming a migraine.

Now, the triggers are everywhere. He cannot walk past a construction site where a generator runs. The sound is immediate, visceral—it transports him back to that cell. He has become hypervigilant. He scans the faces of strangers in the hospital cafeteria, looking for the men who took him. He has rearranged his apartment so that he can see the front door from every room. He sleeps in two-hour intervals, jolted awake by a sound that isn't there. He has stopped dating, stopped going to the symphony he once loved. The noise of crowds feels like an assault.

His work is suffering. He finds himself dissociating during sessions, his mind going blank while a patient speaks. He has prescribed himself a low dose of a benzodiazepine, which he takes before seeing any patient who reminds him of his past. His PCL-5 score is 47, a number he calculated himself, with a cold, clinical detachment. He knows the score is high. He knows he is in trouble. But telling this story, in this room, feels like the most dangerous thing he has ever done. He sits in the chair, hands clasped, and waits for the next question.
